title: Christmas Light Clips Guide: Shingle, Parapet, Universal, Adhesive and Stakes
metaTitle: Christmas Light Clips Guide | Holiday Lights Direct
metaDescription: Which Christmas light clip to use on shingles, gutters, parapets, brick, stucco and walkways, with spacing, clips per 100 ft and removal for Canadian homes.
excerpt: The right clip for every surface on a Canadian home or commercial building, how far apart to place them, how many to order per 100 ft of C9 line, how to take them down at season end, and the shortcuts that damage roofing.
heroAlt: Shingle-tab clips holding a green C9 socket wire along the eave of a snow-dusted Ontario home, with universal clips on the gutter and light stakes lining the walkway below
keyTakeaways: Choose the clip by the surface it mounts to, not by the light: shingle-tab clips for asphalt rooflines, universal clips for gutters and eaves, parapet clips for flat commercial roofs, adhesive clips for brick and stucco, and stakes for pathways.
Clip every socket on a C9 line, which at 12 inch spacing means about 100 clips per 100 ft, and add a few extra for corners and the ones that break.
Clips work by friction and gravity. Nothing should be nailed, screwed or stapled through a shingle, and nothing should lift a shingle tab in freezing weather.
Adhesive clips need a clean, dry surface applied above freezing, and they belong on masonry and hard trim, not on painted wood or vinyl you care about.
Take lines down on a mild day, unclip rather than pull, and store the clips with the runs so next year's install starts with everything in hand.

body.text: Bulbs and wire get all the attention, but the clips are what decide whether a display looks straight from the street, stays up through a January wind and comes down without a roofing bill. Holiday Lights Direct stocks the clip types that professional installers use across Canada, and each one exists because a particular surface needs it. This guide goes surface by surface, then covers spacing, quantities, removal and the shortcuts that damage a roof.
Match the clip to the surface, not the light

Most clips in the trade are designed for C7 and C9 socket wire, the flat cord with a socket every 12 inches, and hold either the cord or the base of the socket. The bulb does not care what clip it is in. What matters is what the clip grips on the building: the edge of a shingle, the lip of a gutter, the cap of a parapet wall, the face of a brick or the ground beside a walkway. Walk the property before you order and note every surface the line will follow, including the transitions where a roofline run drops down a wall to reach the outlet.
Asphalt shingle rooflines: shingle-tab clips

The most common residential surface in Canada is the asphalt shingle roof, and the shingle-tab clip is built for it. A thin, flat tongue slides up under the bottom edge of a shingle tab and the body of the clip hangs below the edge, holding the socket wire so the bulbs sit just under the roofline. The clip relies on the weight of the shingle above and the friction of the granules to stay put; nothing is fastened and nothing is cut. Sighted from the ground, a properly clipped line runs dead straight along the drip edge with every bulb pointing the same way.

Slide the tongue in flat and gently. In cold weather asphalt shingles stiffen and lifting a tab more than a few millimetres can crack the shingle or break the seal strip that glues it to the course below. If a tab will not accept the tongue without lifting, move over a few inches to the next one. Shingle-tab clips also work on the rake edge of a gable where the shingles overhang the trim.
Eaves and gutters: universal clips

Where a home has eavestroughs along the roofline, the gutter lip is often a better mount than the shingles above it, and the universal clip is the tool. It hooks over the front lip of the gutter and holds the socket wire or the socket base in a channel, so the line sits on the face of the gutter. The same clip has a second feature that lets it slide under a shingle tab, which is why it is called universal: one clip in the pouch handles gutters, eaves and shingles on the same house. If you are only buying one clip type for a typical residential job, this is it.
Flat commercial roofs: parapet clips

Commercial buildings, plazas and municipal properties usually have flat roofs with a low parapet wall around the edge, capped with metal flashing. There are no shingles to slide under and, on most buildings, no gutter lip. The parapet clip is shaped to grip the outer edge of that cap flashing and hold the socket wire along the face of the parapet, so the bulbs outline the building from the street. Because parapet runs are long and exposed, use the heavier SPT-2 socket wire, clip every socket and check the flashing edge for sharp burrs that could chafe the jacket.
Drip edges, trim and awkward spots: duckbill clips

Every house has a few places where neither a shingle tab nor a gutter lip is available: a metal drip edge with no gutter, a fascia board, the edge of a porch roof, or a length of trim around a bay window. The duckbill clip is the flexible option for these, with a hinged jaw that closes on the socket wire or the socket base and a mounting end that grips an edge. Check the product page for the exact edges it is designed to grip. Keep a bag of them in the kit for the spots the main clip type cannot reach, and for holding a run to the edge of a garage roof where the shingles are too tight to lift.
Brick, stucco and stone: adhesive clips

Wall surfaces have no edge to clip to, and drilling into brick or stucco for a seasonal display is a bad trade. Adhesive clips are small plastic hooks or channels with a pressure-sensitive pad on the back, sized for mini-light strands and thin cord rather than heavy C9 socket wire. They are what you use to outline a window in brick, run a mini-light strand along a stucco column or carry a cord across a stone step. On a masonry wall, aim for the flat face of a brick rather than the mortar joint, which is rougher and often dusty.

items: Clean the spot with a dry cloth and let it dry fully. Dust, frost and efflorescence on brick all defeat the adhesive.
Apply above freezing. Most pressure-sensitive adhesives need a mild temperature to bond, so put adhesive clips up on a warm October afternoon rather than a cold November night.
Press firmly for a few seconds and leave the clip empty for a while before loading the cord.
Use adhesive clips for mini-light strands and light cord only. C9 socket wire is too heavy for a small pad on a cold wall.
Avoid painted wood, vinyl siding and any finish you care about; the pad can lift paint or leave residue when it comes off.

body.text: Pathways, driveways and garden beds: light stakes

Ground runs need their own mount, and a light stake is a plastic spike with a clip at the top that holds the socket wire or the bulb base above the grass. Push a stake in beside the walkway every socket or every second socket, and the line stands off the ground where snow and foot traffic are less likely to bury or crush it. Get stakes in before the ground freezes; a hammer breaks them. Keep the ground run on its own plug pair so it can be unplugged and lifted when the snow shovel comes out.
Spacing and how many clips per 100 ft

The professional standard on a roofline is one clip per socket. With 12 inch socket spacing that is about 100 clips per 100 ft of C9 line. Every-socket clipping is what keeps the line straight in daylight, because any socket left unclipped droops between its neighbours and the whole run reads as scalloped from the street. On a sheltered straight eave some homeowners clip every second socket to save time, but the first wind flips the unclipped bulbs sideways. Corners, peaks and the run in and out of a gable should always be clipped at every socket.

items: Roofline C9 runs on shingles or gutters: 100 clips per 100 ft, plus about 10 percent extra for corners, breakage and the ones that fall in the snow.
Parapet runs: 100 per 100 ft, and do not skip sockets on an exposed commercial edge.
Ground runs on stakes: 50 to 100 per 100 ft depending on how straight you want the line and how much snow you expect on it.
Mini-light strands on adhesive clips: one clip every 12 to 18 inches, plus one at every change of direction.

body.text: Order clips by the line, not by the bulb: count the sockets on each run, add them up, and round up to the next pack size. Clips are cheap compared with a second trip up the ladder to fix a sagging section.
Taking it all down at season end

Removal is where most damage happens. Pick a mild, dry day when the shingles are pliable and there is no frost on the granules. Unplug everything first. Then work along the line unclipping each socket from its clip rather than pulling the wire and letting the clips tear free: a yanked shingle-tab clip can take a corner of shingle with it, and a yanked gutter clip can bend the gutter lip.

items: Slide shingle-tab clips straight out the way they went in. If one is frozen in, leave it for a warmer day rather than prying.
Leave the clips on the socket wire when you coil the run. The clips store with the line and go back up in the same positions next year, which is the single biggest time saver on a re-install.
Peel adhesive clips off slowly, pulling the pad flat along the surface rather than straight out. Warm the pad with your hand or a hair dryer on a cold day.
Pull light stakes straight up before the ground freezes hard, or wait for a thaw.
Label each coiled run with its location on a piece of tape at the male plug end before it goes in the bin.

body.text: What damages roofing, and what does not

items: Nails, screws and staples through shingles or flashing. Every one is a hole that will leak, and staples through a cord also damage the jacket. Never fasten a line this way.

Lifting shingle tabs in freezing weather. Cold asphalt cracks and the seal strip breaks, and a shingle with a broken seal lifts in the next storm. Slide clips in gently on a mild day, or move to a gutter clip.
Walking on a frosted or snow-covered roof. Beyond the fall risk, boots scuff granules off frozen shingles. Work from a ladder or a lift at the edge.
Pulling wire to remove clips. Unclip each socket by hand.
Heavy cord on adhesive pads. It will fall, and it may take paint with it.

Leaving seasonal clips and runs up all year. The plastic degrades in summer sun and shingles hold moisture under the cord. For a year-round outline, use a permanent LED roofline kit on aluminum track instead.

What does not damage roofing: properly seated shingle-tab clips, universal clips on the gutter lip, parapet clips on the cap flashing and stakes in the lawn. Used correctly, all of them come off in January and leave no trace.

body.text: The right clip on the right surface is what separates a display that looks installed from one that looks hung. Holiday Lights Direct carries shingle-tab, universal, parapet, duckbill and adhesive clips along with light stakes, and ships them from London, Ontario across Canada with free shipping on orders over the threshold shown on the product page. faq.q: Which clip should I use on an asphalt shingle roof?
faq.a: A shingle-tab clip, which slides flat under the bottom edge of a shingle tab and holds the C9 socket wire below the roofline without any fasteners. If the home has gutters, a universal clip on the gutter lip is often easier and just as neat.

faq.q: How many light clips do I need per 100 feet?
faq.a: About 100 for a C9 line clipped at every socket, since the sockets are 12 inches apart, plus roughly 10 percent extra for corners and breakage. Ground runs on stakes need 50 to 100 per 100 ft, and mini-light strands on adhesive clips need one every 12 to 18 inches.

faq.q: What clip works on a flat commercial roof?
faq.a: A parapet clip. It grips the metal cap flashing on the parapet wall and holds the socket wire along the face of the building. Clip every socket, use SPT-2 socket wire and check the flashing edge for burrs before running the line.

faq.q: Can I use adhesive clips for C9 lights on brick?
faq.a: Adhesive clips are for mini-light strands and light cord, not heavy C9 socket wire. On brick, apply them to the flat face of a clean, dry brick above freezing, press firmly and let them set before loading the cord.

faq.q: Will Christmas light clips damage my shingles?
faq.a: Not when used properly. Shingle-tab and universal clips rely on friction and gravity and leave no holes. Damage comes from lifting tabs in freezing weather, walking on a frosted roof, nailing or stapling lines, and pulling wire to yank clips free at removal.
